HomeEssentials Inc. - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the HomeEssentials Inc. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss HomeEssentials Inc.'s results for the Q3. Joining me on today’s call are David Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to David.

David Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Emily. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report HomeEssentials Inc.'s performance for the Q3. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Key highlights this quarter include exceptional labor productivity and store payroll leverage, accelerating omnichannel initiatives like BOPIS and curbside pickup, robust e-commerce sales growth year-over-year, and advanced strategies for inventory optimization across our 1,250 stores nationwide. These efforts underscore our ability to drive efficiency in a brick-and-mortar world while capitalizing on digital synergies.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa to provide more details on our financial results.

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, David. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the Q3.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $6.8 billion, a 4.2% increase compared to the same period last year, driven by a mix of 2.8% same-store sales growth, e-commerce acceleration, and contributions from 15 net new stores in high-growth markets.

Gross margin was 39.8%, expanding 120 basis points year-over-year, primarily driven by improved product mix, disciplined pricing, labor productivity gains, and effective inventory management that reduced shrinkage and optimized turns.

Operating expenses were $2.2 billion, representing 32.4% of revenue, reflecting leverage from higher sales volumes and productivity tools, partially offset by targeted investments in technology.

Net income was $420 million, or $1.48 per diluted share, surpassing our guidance midpoint.

We generated $520 million in cash flow from operations, supporting share repurchases of $150 million and capex of $220 million focused on omnichannel and supply chain enhancements.

Inventory levels are currently well-optimized at $1.85 billion, down 8% year-over-year, with turnover at 5.8x and days inventory outstanding at 63 days—freeing up significant working capital.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

To give you more context on the drivers behind these results, let me expand on the key operational areas David highlighted, starting with labor costs and store payroll leverage, which has been a major focus for our brick-and-mortar operations where labor is our largest controllable expense at the store level, typically 16-20% of sales industry-wide.

In Q3, store payroll as a percentage of sales improved to 18.5%, a 70 basis point decline from 19.2% in Q3 2023 and 40 basis points better sequentially from Q2 2024. This marked our strongest quarterly leverage in three years, providing about $28 million in favorability against plan and adding roughly 25 basis points to gross margin expansion. Year-to-date, we're at 18.7% of sales, up 60 basis points year-over-year.

Contextually, sales per labor hour, or SPLH, rose 5.2% year-over-year to $142 per hour across our 1,250 stores—surpassing the industry average of 3-4% as shared by peers like Target and Kohl's. Total store labor dollars grew just 1.8% year-over-year, or $42 million, despite 4.5% wage inflation in base hourly rates. With sales up 6.1%, this created classic positive leverage, expanding store operating margin by 110 basis points to 9.8%.

The drivers included disciplined staffing and productivity improvements. We kept headcount flat at 85,000 store associates year-over-year, even with 15 net new stores in Sunbelt markets like Texas and Florida. Full-time equivalent hours per store week dropped 2.1% to 1,850, aided by precise scheduling. Schedule adherence hit 92%, up from 87% last year, via rollout of the UKG Dimensions AI scheduling platform to 85% of stores. This matches labor to traffic patterns, cutting overstaffing in shoulder hours by 15%—for instance, reducing midday idle time in paint and lumber departments from 25% to under 10%.

Technical initiatives are also scaling: 70% of stores feature expanded self-checkout with AI fraud detection, trimming front-end cashier hours by 8%, akin to Walmart's approach. In competitive categories like appliances and flooring against Home Depot and Lowe's, associate tablet workflows for curbside fulfillment improved pick efficiency by 22%, enabling flexible picker hours. Our internal labor productivity index stands at 112 against a 2019 baseline, up from 105 year-over-year.

Regionally, results showed brick-and-mortar dynamics: Sunbelt stores (35% of base) saw SPLH up 7.8% to $158, with 120 basis points leverage to 17.2% of sales amid 12% comp traffic from migration and home improvement. Northeast stores (20%) achieved 40 basis points leverage at 20.1%, pressured by high-wage states like California and New York with AB 1228 hikes to $20/hour, union activity, and 6% inflation—SPLH averaged $148. Midwest and Southeast hit 90-100 basis points leverage.

Moving forward, with industry wages up 4.8% per BLS, we're planning 4.2% for FY24, but our advantages lie in cross-training and omnichannel ties—over 60% of associates handle BOPIS and ship-from-store, up 18% year-over-year without headcount growth. A $15 million FY24 investment in RFID for 200 pilot stores targets another 3-5% SPLH gain by minimizing stockouts. We anticipate 50-75 basis points leverage in the back half with 3-5% comps, mitigated by our tech against West Coast laws or soft traffic—mirroring Costco and TJX successes.

Next, our omnichannel initiatives continue as a growth cornerstone for HomeEssentials Inc., a leading brick-and-mortar player with 1,250 stores in home improvement, furnishings, and essentials—blending big-box scale like Home Depot with Wayfair-like physical presence. These focus on seamless BOPIS, curbside pickup, and ship-from-store via a unified tech stack boosting sales and traffic.

Headline metrics show momentum: Omnichannel fulfillment (digital orders via stores) hit 28% of total e-commerce GMV, up from 22% last year and 18% in Q3 2022—a 27% year-over-year rise contributing $285 million to $1.4 billion in digital sales. Digital penetration reached 20% of company revenue, beating 15-16% guidance and eyeing 18-20% FY24. BOPIS grew 32% to $162 million (57% of omnichannel), curbside 41% to $98 million (34%), ship-from-store 55% to $25 million via same-day pilots.

These drive profitability: Omnichannel AOV is 24% higher at $145 vs. $117 for pure e-comm, with 4.2% conversion (double NRF's 2.1%). Fulfillment costs fell to 8.2% of sales from 9.5%, lifting digital gross margin to 42.3%, up 110 basis points despite apparel softness.

BOPIS leads, enabled in 92% of stores (up from 85%), with RFID smart shelves in 450 sites offering 98% SKU accuracy—QR app reservations, 96% on-time, turning online browsers into 1.7x basket store explorers per Verkada data.

Curbside targets millennials/Gen Z (62% users, up from 55%), expanded to 1,100 stores with geofencing and contactless pay—AOV up 18% to $132 via bundling, 28% enter stores post-pickup for 15% dwell increase.

Our $150 million HomeEssentials Unified Platform on AWS/Manhattan WMS enables 50-mile inventory pooling, cutting Dallas-Fort Worth stockouts 37% via Blue Yonder AI with weather/events. Voice pilots with Alexa in 200 Pacific Northwest stores leverage high adoption.

Regions vary positively: Sunbelt 35% growth (Phoenix BOPIS 22% of sales), Northeast 24% (Uber partnerships in 50 NYC/Boston stores), Midwest 19% (Chicago ship-from-store 45%), Canada 26% (Tim Hortons-tied curbside).

This builds moat vs. Amazon/Wayfair—68% consumers prefer hybrid per surveys, matching McKinsey's 75% retention. Loyalty gives 2x points, 41% higher repeats, $2.3 billion LTV. $1 invested yields $4.20 EBITDA, 28% ROI.

Ahead: 98% BOPIS coverage Q4, same-day curbside in 800 stores, 20 micro-fulfillment by YE25—capturing 4.2% CAGR $1.2T market per Deloitte.

Omnichannel drove 15% of Q3 comps, de-risking our model.

Shifting to e-commerce sales growth year-over-year, which remains central to our omnichannel shift. E-commerce net sales hit $1.45 billion, up 32% year-over-year—outpacing retail's 18-22% per NRSC/Digital Commerce 360.

Excluding marketplace (up 15% to $280 million GMV in kitchen/seasonals), total digital is 28% of sales, from 22% last year.

Trends: Mobile 62% traffic (from 55%), app downloads +45% post-relaunch. AOV +12% to $145 via Adobe AI bundling/loyalty (18M members, +24%). Conversions to 4.2% from 3.6% with AR for furniture/appliances.

U.S. +35% to $1.1B (Northeast/Sunbelt same-day 22% via DoorDash/Instacart). Europe +25% to €220M (UK/Germany sites, VAT headwinds). Canada/Mexico +18% (BOPIS 28% of orders).

Profitably: E-comm gross margin +210 bps to 42.5% (vs. stores' 38.2%) via less discounting/Manhattan WMS. CAC -14% to $28 via TikTok/Pinterest (5.8x ROAS on private label).

Future: $150M Q4 capex for Atlanta/Dallas DCs (95% next-day for 80% U.S.), Salesforce headless for videos/live-streams (3x apparel uplift). Q4 growth 28-32%, FY digital ~$5.2B vs. peers' <20%.

Validates "Stores as Hubs": 42% online fulfilled via stores/BOPIS, +15% repeats.

Finally, our inventory optimization strategies are fueling profitability against Amazon/Shein. Inventory turnover rose to 5.8x from 4.9x, DIO to 63 from 75 days—freeing $285M working capital for remodels/DCs. Shrinkage 1.2% (-30 bps), top-quartile vs. NRF's 4.5x average.

Playbook: AI demand sensing on Blue Yonder/Manhattan ingests POS/weather/sentiment data—92% accuracy at SKU-store-week (from 82%), avoiding $45M 2022 markdowns.

SKU rationalization: -18% to 37,000 SKUs, private label 28% at 7.2x. Localized: Northeast coldwear +15% SKUs (12% better sell-through), Sunbelt summer shift (-40% stockouts).

JIT/VMI: 65% perishables suppliers auto-replenish (safety stock -22%), apparel 2-week leads from Vietnam/Bangladesh. Inventory-to-sales 28% vs. 34% average.

RFID 85% stores (Avery chipless, 99.5% visibility, -35% count labor/-18% OOS). IoT in 10 DCs flags spoilage. Blockchain pilots for electronics.

Omnichannel: SFS 22% online, BOPIS 35% (+50%), dynamic slotting +14% traffic conversion.

Regions: Europe 250 stores post-Primark, micro-DCs vs. Brexit (-9% sell-through gain). Asia-Pacific 180 stores 6.4x via Shenzhen JIT. U.S. Midwest 95% in-stock.

Aligns trends: +25% staples velocity. Sustainability: -17% waste. AI pricing +8% slow-mover recovery.

Expect 10-15% DIO cut FY24, $150M FCF, $45M capex (2.1x ROI). Risks mitigated by dual-sourcing.

These efforts expanded gross margin 120 bps to 42.1%, outpacing rivals.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning, team. Can you provide more color on the impact of softening consumer spending amid inflation on your sales mix?

David Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, John. Absolutely, inflation has pressured discretionary categories, but our value-focused private labels and omnichannel convenience have helped. BOPIS and curbside drove higher AOV and traffic conversion, with omnichannel contributing 15% to comps. We're seeing resilience in essentials and home improvement in Sunbelt markets, offsetting Northeast softness. Overall, this positions us well as consumers trade down to trusted brick-and-mortar hybrids.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Sarah Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Sarah Lee (Morgan Stanley):
Thanks. What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Hi Sarah. We're guiding to 2-4% same-store sales growth for Q4, assuming stable macros. This factors in holiday tailwinds, 28-32% e-commerce acceleration, and continued 50-75 bps payroll leverage. Omnichannel should add another 1-2 points, with inventory agility supporting in-stocks above 95%.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Mike Patel (JPMorgan):
Great, thanks. On inventory, with Red Sea issues lingering, how are you managing risks and what's the outlook for turnover?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Hi Mike. We've dual-sourced with 40% West Coast routing, minimizing disruptions. Our AI forecasting and RFID have us at 92% accuracy, targeting 6.2x turnover FY24. DIO compression of 10-15% will deliver $150 million extra FCF. Pilots like blockchain add resilience for high-value items. We're ahead of peers and confident.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes today's questions.

David Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
